translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>When the Emperor heard of it, he took pity on him, established Luan as King of Sishui, and had the Chancellor and Senior Scribe cast into prison. In the third month, silk fabric was bestowed upon those selected by the commanderies and kingdoms for conduct and righteousness, including Han Fu of Zhuo Commandery and four others, fifty bolts per person, and they were sent home. An edict declared: "We regret to wear them out with the burdens of official duties."

<note>Deng Zhan states: "The Emperor took pity and felt grief for Han Fu and the others, and could not bear to wear them out with labor and service in official duties."</note>

"Let them devote themselves to cultivating filial piety and brotherly respect in order to instruct their local communities. Let the commanderies and counties regularly grant them sheep and wine in the first month. If any among them meets with misfortune, grant them a single suit of clothing and quilts, and sacrifice to them with a <term>zhonglao</term> <gloss>secondary sacrificial offering of sheep and pig</gloss>."

<note>Yan Shigu states: "Fortunate means auspicious and avoiding misfortune; hence death is referred to as misfortune. A suit refers to a complete set, like saying a pair or set today. The <term>zhonglao</term> is the lesser offering <term>shaolao</term>, referring to a sheep and a pig."</note>

The Di people of Wudu rebelled.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The character <term>Di</term> has the fanqie pronunciation of <term>ding</term> and <term>xi</term>."</note>

The Commander of the Capital Gendarmes <term>Zhi Jinwu</term> Ma Shi Jian and Marquis of Long'e Han Zeng were dispatched.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The surname was Mashi and the personal name was Jian. For Long'e, editions of the Hanshu sometimes write the character <term>Luo</term>. The Table of Meritorious Officials and Marquises states that Han Tuodang, Marquis Zhuang of Gonggao, had a son named Gui who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Longluo. In the fifth year of the Yuanding era he was stripped of rank due to the gold offering offense. In the first year of the Houyuan era, Gui's younger brother's son Zeng succeeded to the enfeoffment as Marquis of Longluo. Xun Yue's Han Annals uses the character <term>E</term> for all instances of Longluo. Cui Hao says that <term>luo</term> is pronounced like <term>luo</term>."</note>

<note>Former Han Annals commentary by Ciding: "...serving others has three grades..."</note>

<summary>Emperor Zhao restores the Kingdom of Sishui for the posthumous prince Luan, punishes negligent officials, rewards virtuous elders with stipends, and dispatches generals to quell a Di rebellion in Wudu.</summary>
<keywords>Emperor Zhao, Sishui, Luan, Han Fu, Zhuo Commandery, filial piety, zhonglao, Wudu, Di rebellion, Ma Shi Jian, Han Zeng, Long'e, Yan Shigu, Deng Zhan</keywords>

<note>Yan Shigu says: ...the pronunciation is like the character <term>yi</term> combined with <term>fan</term>, as noted above. The two characters are combined.</note>

### Volume 94, Part 2

<note>Yan Shigu says: The character <term>hui</term> <gloss>beak/jaw</gloss> is pronounced like <term>xu</term> combined with <term>hui</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

By the beginning of the Benshi reign <note>73–70 BCE</note>, the Xiongnu harbored treacherous and recalcitrant ambitions.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Jie</term> <gloss>obstinate/stubborn</gloss> means hard and rebellious. It signifies that they arose in disobedience.</note>

They wished to plunder the Wusun and violate the Han princess. Thereupon, five generals were dispatched leading an expeditionary army of 150,000 cavalry to hunt down the enemy across the south, while the Marquis of Changluo led 50,000 cavalry from the Wusun to strike awe throughout their western border. Both forces reached their agreed rendezvous points and returned.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>pledge/rendezvous</gloss> means good faith; it refers to the appointed place.</note>

At that time, they captured little.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Xian</term> <gloss>rare</gloss> means few; it is pronounced like <term>xian</term> combined with <term>jian</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

They merely displayed their martial prowess and manifested the might of Han forces like thunder and wind. Although they marched out and returned empty-handed, two generals were nevertheless executed for their failures. Therefore, the northern barbarians did not submit, and the Central Plains could not yet rest easy on high pillows.

When it came to the Yuankang and Shenjue eras <note>65–58 BCE</note>, great spiritual virtue and majestic grace spread widely, while internal turmoil erupted within the Xiongnu. Five Chanyu competed for the throne. Rizhu and Huhanye brought their state to submit in desperation, prostrating themselves and declaring themselves subjects.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Fu</term> <gloss>prostrate</gloss> is pronounced like <term>pu</term> combined with <term>bei</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

Yet the Han court still maintained the strategy of loose rein <note>jimi</note>, not assuming arbitrary and total control over them.

<note>Yan Shigu says: The character <term>zhuan</term> is identical with <term>zhuan</term> <gloss>monopolize/dominate</gloss>. <term>Zhuanzhi</term> <gloss>exclusive control</gloss> refers to reducing them completely to subjects and bondservants.</note>

<summary>Following minor frontier campaigns against the Xiongnu during the Benshi reign, internal civil war fractured the Xiongnu under five rival Chanyu, prompting Huhanye to submit to Han authority under the loose-rein policy.</summary>
<keywords>Hanshu, Xiongnu, Wusun, Huhanye Chanyu, Benshi, Yuankang, Shenjue, Yan Shigu, Jimi policy</keywords>

translation:
<header>Volume 95</header>

Zhu said: "Our state has only recently suffered invasion. The envoy should depart; Hu is even now preparing day and night to enter the capital and have audience with the Son of Heaven."

After Zhu departed, his ministers remonstrated with Hu, saying: "The Han raised an army to execute Ying, but in truth they also acted to intimidate Southern Yue. Moreover, the late king stated that in serving the Son of Heaven, one should strive not to fail in protocol, but the crucial point is that one must not be seduced by flattering words into entering the capital for an audience."
<gloss>Shigu says: "Chu" means to entice or induce. It means one must not be enticed and persuaded by sweet words to enter the Han court. The character is pronounced like the fanqie of xian and yu.</gloss>
"If you enter the capital for an audience, you will never be able to return; this would be the circumstance that brings ruin to our state."

Thereupon Hu claimed illness and ultimately did not go to the capital for an audience. More than ten years later, Hu fell genuinely and gravely ill. Crown Prince Yingqi requested permission to return home. When Hu died, he was given the posthumous title King Wen.

Yingqi succeeded to the throne. He immediately concealed the imperial seals of his predecessors, the Martial Emperor <note>Zhao Tuo</note> and the Civil Emperor <note>Zhao Hu</note>.
<gloss>Li Qi says: He discarded their usurped imperial titles.</gloss>

During his time in Chang'an, Yingqi had taken a woman of the Jiu clan from Handan as his wife.
<gloss>Shigu says: Jiu is pronounced like the fanqie of ju and qiu.</gloss>
She bore a son named Xing. When Yingqi ascended the throne, he submitted a memorial requesting that the woman of the Jiu clan be established as queen and that Xing be made his heir. The Han repeatedly sent envoys

<summary>Ministers convince King Hu of Southern Yue not to visit the Han court out of fear he will be detained, leading him to feign illness until his death, whereupon his heir Zhao Yingqi assumes the throne, conceals the former royal usurpation seals, and seeks Han recognition for his northern wife and son.</summary>
<keywords>Zhao Hu, Yan Zhu, King Wen of Southern Yue, Zhao Yingqi, Zhao Xing, Jiu clan, Handan, Hanshu, Siku Quanshu, Yan Shigu, Li Qi, Western Han</keywords>

On the day <term>yihai</term>, the moon was eclipsed in the evening and was not seen. An earthquake occurred in Longxi. In summer, there was a drought. Zhong, the Marquis of Heyang, died.

<gloss>Yan Shigu stated: 'He was an elder brother of Emperor Gaozu and the father of Liu Pi, the King of Wu.'</gloss>

In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day <term>xinwei</term>, Chancellor of State Xiao He died.

<gloss>Yan Shigu stated: 'This refers to Xiao He.'</gloss>

In the third year, in spring, 146,000 men and women from within six hundred <term>li</term> <gloss>Chinese miles</gloss> of Chang'an were conscripted to build the city walls of Chang'an. After thirty days, the work was halted.

<gloss>Master Zheng stated: 'Only one side of the city wall was built; therefore, the work ceased quickly.'</gloss>

A daughter of the imperial clan was designated as a princess and given in marriage to the <term>Chanyu</term> <gloss>supreme ruler</gloss> of the Xiongnu.

In summer, in the fifth month, Yao, the ruler of Minyue, was established as the King of Donghai.

<gloss>Ying Shao stated: 'Yao was a descendant of Goujian, King of Yue. He led the troops of the Hundred Yue tribes to assist Emperor Gaozu; therefore, he was enfeoffed with Donghai. Donghai lay southeast of Wu Commandery, bordering the sea.' Yan Shigu stated: 'This is the modern region of Quanzhou.'</gloss>

In the sixth month, twenty thousand convict laborers and bondservants belonging to the tributary kings and full marquises were mobilized to build the city walls of Chang'an. In autumn, in the seventh month, a fire broke out in the metropolitan stables. Zhao Tuo, the King of Nanyue, declared himself a vassal and offered tribute.

<gloss>Yan Shigu stated: 'Tuo is pronounced with the fanqie spelling tu-he.' Ci Ding stated: 'The affair was thus brought to completion.'</gloss>

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>had their assigned duties.

<gloss>Brave imperial palace guards <note>original: "huben"</note> were ministers who maintained the night watch and garrisoned the palace. Attendants of robes <note>original: "zhuiyi"</note> were officials in charge of imperial attire; *zhui* <note>original: "贅"</note> means to stitch or attach <note>original: "綴"</note>, pronounced with the initial and final of *zhi* and *rui*. The *Classic of Documents* states: "Attendants of imperial robes and brave imperial palace guards." Gatekeepers and eunuch chamberlains <note>original: "hunyin"</note> as well as private apartment eunuchs <note>original: "hunsi"</note> were both eunuch officials. The *Rites of Zhou* includes gatekeepers and chamberlain eunuchs. "With halberds arrayed on the palace steps" means clutching halberds while standing upon the palace steps. "A hundred ranks" indicates great numbers. *You* means place or that which; *si* means to take charge of. For rhyme, it is pronounced like *si* <note>meaning to watch over or wait upon</note>.</gloss>

Round guard lodges in a thousand ranks, patrol lanes interlaced like patterned silk.

<gloss>Guard lodges refer to the lodging quarters of the imperial night guard stationed around the palace perimeter. "A thousand ranks" signifies great abundance. The "Statutes for the Palace Guard" in the *Records of the Grand Historian* state: "Round guard lodges were established with troops under exceedingly strict discipline." Patrol lanes were paths for making surveillance rounds. "Interlaced like patterned silk" means crisscrossing. The *History of the Former Han* states: "The Commander of the Capital Guards held charge over patrols and inspections in the capital city."</gloss>

Imperial carriage thoroughfares wind and turn; extended roadways and soaring pavilions rise aloft.

<gloss>The *Phonetic Meanings of the History of the Former Han* says: "Carriage thoroughfares refer to raised corridors and elevated walkways." *Tu* <note>original: "涂"</note> also means road <note>original: "塗"</note>; these ancient characters were interchangeable.</gloss>

Reaching out from the Weiyang Palace to connect with the Gui Palace, extending northward past the Mingguang Palace and linking across to the Changle Palace; crossing over stepped pathways and rising above the western city wall; joined together with the Jianzhang Palace as an outer annex; erecting the Phoenix Watchtowers of the Jade Gate, where high upon the ridge beams roost golden sparrows.

<gloss>The Weiyang Palace lay in the west, while the Changle Palace lay in the east. The Gui Palace and Mingguang Palace lay in the north. This describes elevated walkways interconnecting them. *Deng* refers to the flight of steps, pronounced with the initial and final of *ding* and *deng*. *Yong* means the city wall. *Hun* means unified together. The Jianzhang Palace was situated west of the walled city; *shu* means connected. The *History of the Former Han* states: "To the east of the Jianzhang Palace stood the Phoenix Watchtower Gate, over twenty *zhang* high; to its south stood the Jade Gate and its annexes." The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Guling* refers to the highest vantage point atop a palace hall." *Gu* is pronounced like *gu*; *ling* is pronounced like... <note>original: "欠三句半之旨", the commentary text breaks off here with three and a half sentences missing</note></gloss>

<summary>This page continues the Ban Gu commentary on the capital palaces and guard system, detailing the royal bodyguards, eunuch officers, night watchposts, and elevated covered corridors connecting the Weiyang, Changle, Gui, Mingguang, and Jianzhang palaces.</summary>
<keywords>imperial guards, huben, zhuiyi, eunuchs, palace lodges, Weiyang Palace, Changle Palace, Gui Palace, Mingguang Palace, Jianzhang Palace, Phoenix Watchtowers, elevated walkways</keywords>

Has anyone ever not been enabled <note>to perform the sacrifices</note>, relying merely on bamboo and silk writings without magnifying laws and standards, or leaving behind texts without performing the Feng and Shan? How could it be only with regard to me that this alone is omitted?

*Yi* means *wei* <note>an initial particle, "now" or "contemplating"</note>. *Suigu* is like *yuangu* <gloss>profound antiquity</gloss>. The *Songs of Chu* <note>original: "Chuci"</note> states: "At the beginning of profound antiquity..." *Li* means to arrive. This means: from profound antiquity down to the present. "Those who have undertaken" refers to those who performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices. The *Records of the Grand Historian* <note>original: "Shiji"</note> states that Guan Zhong said: "From ancient times, seventy-two rulers performed the Feng and Shan." Adding Emperor Wu and Emperor Guangwu, they make seventy-four rulers. *Bi* means to cause or enable. Possessing the realm under Heaven without being enabled to perform the Feng and Shan, while relying merely on writings upon bamboo and silk: there has never been one who magnified laws and standards, or left behind literary compositions, who omitted the Feng and Shan sacrifices.

*Tai* means me or myself. "How could it be with regard to me that this alone is omitted?"

At this time, the Sage Sovereign had already concentrated his refined spirit and wandered in contemplation, gathering all literary arts. Repeatedly he consulted the gathered scholars and took counsel with venerable elders, deliberating with them upon the deep source of the Way and Virtue, and examining the vast thicket of benevolence and righteousness, in hope that the primal auspicious tokens would arrive.

"Sage Sovereign" refers to Emperor Zhang. *Yu* means to inform; *zi* means to deliberate and counsel. Because the Way, Virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are what people constantly practice, they are compared here to drink and food. "Deep source" and "vast thicket" are metaphors for profound depth. *Yuan* means Heaven. *Fu* means auspicious omen. The *Classic of Poetry* states: "The meats and dried fruits are set out in order." *He* <note>覈</note> also means dried fruits and seeds <note>核</note>, referring to the category of fruits.

Having already achieved the upright words of the feudal lords, he thoroughly examined the profound reflections of the Five Divinations. About to weave together myriad...

Jia Xu, courtesy name Wenhe, was a native of Guzang in Wuwei. In his youth, no one recognized his abilities, except Yan Zhong of Hanyang, who found him extraordinary and said that Xu possessed the marvelous talent of Liang and Ping <note>Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, chief strategists to Han founder Liu Bang</note>.

The <term>Jiuzhou Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals of the Nine Provinces</gloss> states:
In the first year of Zhongping <note>184 CE</note>, General of Chariots and Cavalry Huangfu Song crushed the Yellow Turbans, and his prestige shook the realm.

Yan Zhong, having been dismissed as Magistrate of Xindu, sought to persuade Song, saying: "That which is difficult to obtain yet easy to lose is opportunity. That which arrives and allows no hesitation is a turning point. Therefore, the sage always acts according to the times, and the wise necessarily take advantage of turning points to launch their actions. Now, General, you have encountered a rare fortune and stepped upon an easily resolved turning point. Yet if you walk upon fortune without grasping it, and face a turning point without acting, how will you enjoy great renown?"

Song said: "What do you mean?"

Zhong replied: "The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism; the common people align with capability. Therefore, one who achieves extraordinary merit does not accept reward from an ordinary ruler. Now, General, you were granted the battle-axe in early spring and gathered your success in late winter. Your military movements were like spirits, and your plans never required a second calculation. Within ten days, divine troops swept like lightning. Assaulting fortifications was easier than snapping dry branches, and overthrowing enemies was swifter than pouring hot water upon snow. Rolling across seven provinces, you slaughtered three hundred and sixty thousand troops, utterly leveling the army of Yellow Turbans and removing the calamity of wickedness and harm. Some seal their doors and carve stones, turning south to declare themselves king."

<summary>Xun You is posthumously honored as Marquis Jing, followed by the introduction of Jia Xu, whose early genius was recognized by Yan Zhong as comparable to Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, leading into Yan Zhong urging Huangfu Song to seize power after crushing the Yellow Turbans.</summary>

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>falling short of nine tenths of an inch, reaching only two tenths, or four or five tenths, this constitutes deficiency. When failing to reach a full inch behind the barrier, manifesting at only eight tenths, or five or six tenths, this constitutes deficiency. 

When the primary vessels govern the illness, there is harmony. 

When the illness is contracted within the sinews and bone marrow, and the pulse is intermittent while also surging, the illness is contracted from wine and sexual indulgence. The reason one knows that after five days an ulcerated swelling would form, and after eight days he would vomit pus and die, is that when examining his pulse, the lesser <term>yang</term> <gloss>active, exterior bodily principle</gloss> had begun to alternate. An alternating pulse indicates a disease of the primary vessel. When the illness passes, it moves to the human body; entering the human body, it moves into the collateral vessels governing the illness. At that time, the lesser yang pulse had first reached one tenth of an inch at the barrier position. Therefore, there was internal heat, but the pus had not yet erupted. When it reached five tenths of an inch, it reached the boundary of the lesser yang. 

<note>Collected Explanations: Xu Guang says: 'One' is also written as 'tenth'. The later chapter states that the liver and heart are five tenths of an inch apart, which is why it is said that after five days it is exhausted.</note> <note>Correct Meaning: Wang Shuhe's Pulse Classic states: 'Distinguishing the boundaries of the three gates and what the pulse signs govern: It is said that from the fish border to the high bone, moving backward one inch, the middle is called the cun mouth. From the high bone past the cun to the cubit, it is called the cubit marsh. Therefore it is called cun and cubit. Behind the cubit and in front of the cun is called the barrier. Yang emerges and yin enters, with the barrier serving as the boundary. Yang emerges three tenths of an inch, hence it is called three yin and three yang. Yang is born at the cubit and moves at the cun. Yin is born at the cun and moves at the cubit. The cun governs directing upward to the upper burner, emerging at the head and skin and hair, reaching the hands.'</note>

<summary>This page records Chunyu Yi's diagnostic pulse analysis from the Records of the Grand Historian, explaining how the pulse positions and measurements reveal the progression of internal heat into fatal ulceration, accompanied by commentary on anatomical pulse boundaries from Xu Guang and the Pulse Classic.</summary>
<keywords>Shiji, Chunyu Yi, Wang Shuhe, Xu Guang, pulse diagnosis, lesser yang, barrier pulse, cubit pulse, cun mouth, collateral vessels</keywords>

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>artistic adornment and regular rhythm.

Solitary, delighting in his purpose without tiring of his Way.

<note><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Wang Su says: Music can cause a benevolent man to delight in his purpose in solitude, never growing weary of his Way.</note>

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: This means that King Wu's various generals each rejoiced, symbolizing King Wu's virtue and his ambition for all under Heaven, none tiring of shields, daggers, or the proper Way between ruler and minister.</note>

Completely manifesting his Way, never indulging private desires.

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Because everyone was untiring, the creators of the music modeled every single detail upon them, wishing only to display King Wu's Way in full, not out of personal selfish desire.</note>

Therefore, genuine feelings are revealed and righteousness is established.

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Not tiring of King Wu's Way, their true sentiments were revealed; thus, not indulging private desires, righteousness was established.</note>

The music concludes, and virtue is honored.

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: When the principles of music reach their conclusion, they symbolize deeds of virtue; thus, virtue is honored and made illustrious.</note>

The noble person uses it to delight in goodness, while the common person uses it to halt transgression.

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: The principles of music are complete and sufficient, symbolizing a virtue worthy of reverence. Using this to instruct the world, where could it fail? When the noble person hears it, he delights in goodness; when the common person hears it, he reforms his faults.</note>

Therefore it is said: "Among the ways of nurturing the people, music is greatest."

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: This quotes ancient sayings to conclude that the Way of Music is greatest.</note>

The noble person says: "Ritual and music cannot leave one's person for even an instant."

<note><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: This is Chapter Ten, entitled 'Chapter on Transforming through Music.' Because it transforms the people, it follows the Binmou Jia chapter, making it the tenth chapter. The next text notes: three books of military figures.</note>

<summary>This passage from the Shiji Record of Music explains how martial music cultivates moral purpose, restrains selfish desires, and establishes righteousness among both leaders and commoners. It emphasizes that ritual and music must constantly guide a person, concluding that music is the greatest method for educating and transforming the people.</summary>
<keywords>Shiji, Record of Music, King Wu, Way of Music, virtue, righteousness, ritual and music, moral transformation, Jijie commentary, Zhengyi commentary, Wang Su</keywords>

The following year, the Son of Heaven began his imperial tour of the commanderies and feudal kingdoms. Heading east, he crossed the Yellow River. The Administrator of Hedong did not anticipate the arrival of the imperial procession and was unable to supply provisions; he committed suicide. The procession traveled west and crossed the Long Mountains. The Administrator of Longxi, because the imperial procession had arrived suddenly,

<note>Collected Explanations: Pei Yin notes: The Phonetic Meaning of the Han Shu says: "<term>Yu</term> <gloss>to cross</gloss> means to pass over. <term>Zu</term> <gloss>sudden</gloss> means abrupt and unexpected."</note>

could not provide food for the Son of Heaven's retinue; the Administrator of Longxi committed suicide.

Thereupon, His Majesty traveled north through Xiao Pass. Leading tens of thousands of cavalry, he hunted across the region of Xinqinzhong in order to inspect and train the frontier troops, and then returned. In Xinqinzhong, there were areas of perhaps a thousand <term>li</term> without watchtowers or border patrols.

<note>Collected Explanations: Ru Chun says: "<term>Jiao</term> <gloss>border patrol</gloss> also refers to the class of soldiers who pursue thieves." Jin Zhuo says: "<term>Jiao</term> means border barricades or fortifications." Chen Zan says: "There were neither signal towers nor patrolling border guards; there was no defense prepared for guarding the frontier."</note>

Thereupon, the Grand Administrator of Beidi and those beneath him were executed. The common people were then permitted to graze and breed livestock in the border counties.

<note>Collected Explanations: Pei Yin notes: The Phonetic Meaning of the Han Shu says: "This ordered that the people be allowed to raise livestock in the border counties." Chen Zan says: "Prior to this, in Xinqinzhong there were no inhabitants for a thousand <term>li</term>, as they feared barbarian raiders and did not dare to raise livestock. Once watchtowers and border patrols were established, the people were able to keep livestock."</note>

The government lent them breeding mares, to be returned after three years along with one tenth of the offspring as interest. In this way, the proceeds seized through the denunciation of concealed wealth <note>the <term>gaomin</term> system</note> were used to fill and enrich Xinqinzhong.

<note>Collected Explanations: Ci Ding says: ...</note>

<summary>Emperor Wu toured the empire and inspected the northern frontier at Xinqinzhong, punishing regional officials whose negligence left troops unsupplied or borders undefended. To secure and populate the territory, the court executed negligent administrators, stationed border patrols, and funded livestock colonization through confiscations of concealed wealth.</summary>
